 At 87, Dick Vitale looks toward the future
 Adding to the $126 million he has raised for the V Foundation and announcing college basketball games keeps him motivated.
 By 
 Jay Heater 
 | 1:05 p.m. October 27, 2026 
 Leave a comment 
 -->
 Dick Vitale
 File photo 
 East County 
 Neighbors 
 Share
 Lakewood Ranch's Dick Vitale was sitting behind the desk of his Country Club home, and as grandfathers tend to do, he was talking about the years gone by.
 His past is well-documented, but he doesn't dwell on his coaching days or even those as the face of college basketball broadcasting, all which landed him in multiple halls of fame including the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame (2008); the National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame (2008); and the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame (2018).
 No, most of his stories focused on his formative years, and the love afforded him by his parents, John, a clothing press operator, and Mae, a seamstress. He has wonderful memories of growing up as a Jersey boy, and he stressed that his stable home life put him on the right path and helped him develop into the man he has become.
 "My dad and mom ... their love was unbelievable," he said.
 But after 45 minutes of talking about fond memories, Vitale was up and moving toward the door, the future was calling on a beautiful October morning.
 At 87, Vitale is physically moving slower, but his mind has a whirlwind of objectives.
 After raising $126 million for pediatric cancer research from his previous 21 Dick Vitale Galas, he has to find a way to beat last May's total of $21 million at the 2027 event. He raises his hands skyward and asks, "Where am I getting $21 million?" as if he doesn't know the answer.
 His answer is to be relentless, no matter the circumstances. In a world of uncertainty, he is the poster boy for relentlessly doing good.
 The future pushes Vitale forward when Father Time has other ideas.
 Cancer has threatened to change his plans. He is engaged in his fifth cancer treatment in six years, currently having to undergo regular immunotherapy treatments.
 Vitale was asked if his voice, which sounded a bit strained, was ready for his commitments.
 He gave an incredulous look.
 "It's great," he said of his voice. "Yesterday I did a speaking engagement in St. Pete."
 He speaks to those in his community on a daily basis because he loves to eat in public places and he has his announcing schedule upcoming with his 47th year with ESPN. His contract runs through the 2027-28 season.
 It's full speed ahead, and that's part of the therapy.
 "It's not easy battling cancer," he said. "There is lots of chemo and radiation. But I always think positive and I have faith. If you don't, cancer will eat you alive. My advice is to stay active. If you do nothing, lay in bed, it will eat you up."
 Vitale's current schedule is far beyond just being busy. He just released his All-Rolls-Royce and Diaper Dandy teams, a collection of elite players who have a shot at becoming the faces of college basketball (All-Rolls-Royce) or the next generation of college stars (Diaper Dandies) who are new to the scene.
 His next announcing duty comes Nov. 27 at the Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina, as he will call the North Carolina-West Virginia game. The event is the Dick Vitale Invitational.
 Vitale said he wouldn't accept a broadcasting assignment, or the challenge of raising millions more at his 2027 Dick Vitale Gala, if he didn't expect to go the distance.
 "You need to have that energy and enthusiasm," he said. "So I won't accept any project unless I can finish it. If I can't be me, I won't accept that assignment."
 Tickets for his gala are on sale (DickVitale.com) and he is off to a great start after securing celebrities such as NFL legends Terry Bradshaw and Rob Gronkowski, Notre Dame football coach Marcus Freeman, University of Florida men's basketball coach Todd Golden, Super Bowl champ quarterback Russell Wilson, and ESPN personalities Kevin Negandhi, Jay Harris and Laura Rutledge, among others.
 Vitale has benefitted over the years from benefactors such as Mark and Cindy Pentecost, who have donated millions in matching funds. Mark Pentecost is the founder of It Works!
 "They are two of the most generous, giving people I have ever met," Vitale said of the Pentecosts. "They have hearts of gold. They love helping kids."
 With that, he is out the door to his next task. He has to ask more people if they are willing to support the V Foundation for Cancer Research.
 "You get a lot of rejections, but it motivates me more," he said. "It inspires me. I am never satisfied."
 How long will he continue to raise money for that cause?
 "You have to ask that question to God," he said.
 ____________
 All in the family
 Dick Vitale's energy and enthusiasm in raising money for pediatric cancer research inspires others, including his granddaughter and son-in-law.
 Sydney and Chris Sforzo will run in the New York City Marathon Nov. 1 to raise money for the V Foundation for Cancer Research. Courtesy photo Sydney Sforzo and Christopher Sforzo, who is married to Vitale's daughter, Terri, will run together in the New York City Marathon Nov. 1 with proceeds from their run benefitting the V Foundation for Cancer Research.
 "I knew I had to do something to give back," said Sydney Sforzo, who now works at Edelman, a global communications company in New York City. "Three of my best friends ran in the race and I literally called my dad the day of the marathon last year, and told him we have to do this."
 Neither has run a marathon before, but Sydney Sforzo, who is 25, was a tennis player at Notre Dame while Chris Sforzo is an avid runner who has competed in triathlons.
 "I am faster now than he is," Sydney Sforzo said. "But we push each other regardless of speed. My dad has come to New York three times so we could do long runs (to prepare for the marathon), He is pretty impressive."
 You can donate to their cause at VFoundation.DonorDrive.com/participants/Sydney-Sforzo or VFoundation.DonorDrive.com/participants/31446 
 ____________
 author
 Jay Heater 
 Jay Heater is the managing editor of the East County Observer. Overall, he has been in the business more than 41 years, 26 spent at the Contra Costa Times in the San Francisco Bay area as a sportswriter covering college football and basketball, boxing and horse racing.
